title: Formation and Stability of Cu-Enriched Liquid Phases at the Steel/Oxide Interface: Implications for Surface Hot Shortness in EAF Steels
abstract: Abstract This study investigates the effects of tramp element accumulation on surface hot shortness in electric arc furnace (EAF) steels with an emphasis on the underlying high-temperature interfacial phenomena and process-relevant compositional limits. As scrap utilization increases in EAF steelmaking, the enrichment of tramp elements such as copper becomes unavoidable, necessitating a mechanistic understanding of their role in high-temperature degradation. The chemical compositions of industrial EAF steels (specifically from South Korean practice) were analyzed to quantify the current levels and accumulation trends of tramp elements under high scrap usage. To elucidate the origin of surface hot shortness, high-temperature oxidation experiments were conducted in conjunction with thermodynamic calculations to examine the formation, evolution, and stability of Cu-enriched liquid phases at the steel/oxide scale interface. The results reveal that copper preferentially segregates and forms a low-melting liquid phase at the interface during oxidation, promoting intergranular penetration and surface cracking. The thermodynamic predictions are in good agreement with experimental observations, validating the proposed approach for describing phase stability and interfacial behavior. Based on this mechanistic framework, a copper-equivalent parameter is introduced to quantify the combined effects of tramp elements, and a critical compositional threshold for the onset of surface hot shortness is established. These findings provide a physically grounded criterion for assessing hot shortness susceptibility in scrap-based steels and offer practical guidance for controlling tramp element levels in EAF processes, thereby supporting the reliable operation of high-scrap steelmaking systems.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The increasing use of steel scrap in electric arc furnace (EAF) steelmaking has intensified the accumulation of tramp elements, posing a critical challenge to the production of high-quality steel products. In particular, tramp elements such as Cu and Sn are not readily removed during conventional refining processes and progressively concentrate with repeated recycling. As a result, their influence on high-temperature behavior and surface integrity has become a key limitation in expanding scrap usage in EAF-based steelmaking.

Among the various degradation phenomena associated with tramp elements, surface hot shortness is one of the most critical issues affecting the workability of steel during hot processing. [ 1 ]  This phenomenon is primarily attributed to the formation of a Cu-enriched liquid phase at the steel/oxide scale interface during high-temperature oxidation, due to the preferential oxidation of the steel matrix. [ 2 ]  Due to the limited solubility of Cu in austenite and its low-melting point, this liquid phase can penetrate along austenitic grain boundaries under applied stress, leading to intergranular cracking and surface defects during hot rolling (Figure  1 ). [ 3 , 4 ]  The severity of this phenomenon is strongly dependent on the chemical composition of the steel and the interactions among tramp elements. [ 5 ] Fig. 1 Schematic illustration of copper-induced surface hot shortness in steel during hot working

Previous studies have examined the roles of individual elements in influencing hot shortness behavior. Copper has been identified as the principal contributor due to its tendency to segregate and form a low-melting liquid phase, whereas nickel is known to mitigate this effect by increasing the solubility of Cu in austenite and raising the melting temperature of the Cu-rich liquid phase. [ 6 , 7 ]  In contrast, Sn has been reported to exacerbate hot shortness by lowering both the melting point of the Cu-enriched phase and the solubility of Cu in the matrix. [ 8 ]  Despite these insights, the combined effects of multiple tramp elements on interfacial phase formation and stability remain insufficiently understood, particularly under conditions relevant to industrial EAF processing.

To address this issue, several copper-equivalent expressions have been proposed to quantify the combined influence of tramp elements on hot shortness susceptibility (Table  I ). [ 9 ,  10 ,  11 – 12 ]  These empirical formulations are typically associated with critical threshold values beyond which surface cracking becomes significant. However, considerable discrepancies exist among the reported expressions, primarily due to differences in experimental conditions and the lack of a unified thermodynamic basis. Consequently, a more physically grounded approach is required to establish reliable compositional limits for practical applications. In this study, the effects of tramp element accumulation on surface hot shortness in scrap-based EAF steels are systematically investigated, with a focus on the formation and stability of Cu-enriched liquid phases at the steel/oxide interface. The chemical compositions of industrial EAF steels produced in South Korea are analyzed to characterize current tramp element levels under high scrap utilization. High-temperature oxidation experiments are conducted in conjunction with thermodynamic calculations to elucidate the interfacial phase evolution responsible for hot shortness. Based on the consistency between experimental observations and thermodynamic predictions, a refined copper-equivalent parameter and a corresponding critical compositional threshold are proposed. The results provide a mechanistically grounded framework for evaluating hot shortness susceptibility and offer practical guidance for controlling tramp element levels in EAF steelmaking.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: Nine steel samples were collected from nine EAF steel mills in South Korea, as shown in Figure  2 . These sites are located in Busan, Changwon, Dangjin, Haman, Incheon, and Pohang, and abbreviations were assigned to each region for convenience. Here, the six steelmaking companies are labeled A to F. For instance, a sample labeled “IC-A” denotes a sample from Company A in Incheon. Fig. 2 Geographical distribution of steel scrap from the EAF steelmaking mills, with regional abbreviations indicated

Thirteen elements—copper (Cu), tin (Sn), nickel (Ni), arsenic (As), silicon (Si), manganese (Mn), chromium (Cr), phosphorus (P), lead (Pb), bismuth (Bi), carbon (C), sulfur (S), and nitrogen (N)—were quantitatively analyzed in the nine samples. Cu, Sn, Ni, As, Si, Mn, Cr, P, Pb, and Bi were quantified by using inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES). C and S were quantified using a CS analyzer (CS230, LECO Co., USA), and N was quantified using an ONH analyzer (ONH-2000, ELTRA GmbH, Germany).

sections.heading: Methods
paragraphs: Figure  3  shows a schematic illustration of the experimental apparatus. High-temperature oxidation experiments were conducted at 1100 °C (1373 K) for 1 hour in a vertical tube furnace under an 85 pct N 2 -10 pct CO 2 -5 pct O 2  gas atmosphere, simulating a reheating furnace condition. A sample was cut to dimensions of 10 × 10 × 1 mm 3  and placed at the bottom of an alumina crucible (99.7 pct purity, 40 mm diameter, 55 mm height), located in the center of the reaction tube. The sample was heated under an Ar atmosphere at a heating rate of 3 °C/min(3 K/min) to 300 °C(573 K), and then at 10 °C/min(10 K/min) to 1100 °C(1373 K). Once the experimental temperature was reached, the gas was switched to the reaction gas at a flow rate of 600 mL/min STP(Standard Temperature and Pressure). After the oxidation experiment, the atmosphere was replaced with Ar, and the sample was cooled in the furnace. Detailed heat treatment conditions are presented in Figure  4 . Fig. 3 Schematic illustration of a vertical tube furnace (drawn using gemini) Fig. 4 Heating profile of the sample during the experiment

sections.heading: Analysis
paragraphs: A cross-sectional analysis of the sample was conducted using a field-emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM, SU5000, Hitachi, Japan) coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS, Ultim Max40, Oxford, UK) at an accelerating voltage of 15.0 kV. The upper exposed surface of the sample was analyzed, while the surface of the sample contacting with the alumina crucible was excluded from the analysis.

Thermodynamic calculations were carried out using the FactSage and Thermo-Calc software packages. These software packages can predict the equilibrium phases of samples and the chemical compositions of each phase at elevated temperatures based on their individual compositions and oxygen partial pressures. Oxide formation was mostly investigated with FactSage, while liquid Cu alloy formation was investigated with Thermo-Calc. Equilibrium calculations were performed using the Equilib module of FactSage version 8.3 with the FTstel and FToxid databases. [ 13 , 14 ]  The oxygen partial pressure was controlled by varying the activity of O 2  from 10 −16  to 10 −6.3 . Similarly, equilibrium calculations for liquid Cu alloy were performed with Thermo-Calc using the Equilibrium module version 2025a with the TCOX14 and TCCU6 databases. [ 15 ,  16 – 17 ]  The oxygen partial pressure was adjusted by varying the O 2  activity from 10 −13.3  to 10 −6.3 . For both calculations, the temperature and total pressure were fixed at 1100 °C(1373 K) and 1 atm, respectively. Through these calculations, the equilibrium phases and the elemental composition of the liquid phase at a specific temperature under varying oxygen partial pressures were obtained. This study aimed to evaluate how accurately thermodynamic calculations reproduced the experimental results under conditions closely resembling the actual experimental environment.

sections.heading: Chemical Composition of Scrap-Based Steels
paragraphs: The chemical compositions of the scrap-based steels investigated in this study are summarized in Table  II . Lead and bismuth were below the detection limit (0.002 wt pct) in all samples. The Cu content ranged from 0.20 to 0.35 wt pct, which is consistent with typical values reported for EAF steels. [ 18 ]  Variations in tramp element concentrations, particularly Cu, Sn, and Ni, were observed among the samples, reflecting differences in scrap sources and recycling histories. Compositional variations are particularly important because they directly influence the formation of low-melting interfacial phases during high-temperature processing. In general, Cu and Sn tend to accumulate in post-consumer scrap, [ 19 , 20 ]  whereas Ni is more prevalent in industrial scrap streams. Such variations provide a useful basis for assessing the combined effects of tramp elements on interfacial phase formation and hot shortness susceptibility.

sections.heading: High-Temperature Oxidation and Interfacial Phase Formation
paragraphs: Among the various compositions listed in Table  II , samples PH-A (Figure  5 ) and DJ-F (Figure  6 ) were selected for detailed microstructural observation as representative cases. These two samples were specifically chosen because they exhibit distinct interfacial behaviors despite being oxidized under identical conditions. Sample PH-A represents a composition in which the formation of a continuous liquid phase is suppressed. In contrast, sample DJ-F exhibits pronounced penetration of the Cu-rich liquid phase along prior-austenite grain boundaries. Fig. 5 Cross-sectional FE-SEM backscattered electron (BSE) images of the oxide scale and subsurface region on sample PH-A after high-temperature oxidation: ( a ) Low-magnification overview showing the layered oxide scale structure and steel substrate; yellow boxes indicate regions of interest enlarged in ( b ), ( c ), and ( d ). (b) Outer scale region showing hematite (H) and magnetite (M); the H/M interface (dotted white line) displays an irregular morphology. (c) Wustite-magnetite mixed region (W+M) containing dispersed Cu-rich occlusions (indicated by arrows); inset (c)-1 shows higher-magnification view confirming the fine, discrete morphology of Cu-rich occlusion particles. (d) EDS elemental maps demonstrating Cu and Ni co-enrichment within the occlusion particles, confirming their identity as Cu–Ni alloy phases. ( e ) Steel/scale interface region showing wustite (W) and fayalite (F) phases; inset (e)-1 presents detailed view of the complex oxide assemblage including MnO precipitates, Cr 2 O 3  particles, and fayalite (F) distributed along the interface Fig. 6 Cross-sectional FE-SEM backscattered electron (BSE) images of the oxide scale and subsurface region on sample DJ-F after high-temperature oxidation: ( a ) Low-magnification overview showing the layered oxide scale structure and steel substrate; yellow boxes indicate regions of interest enlarged in ( b ), ( c ), and ( d ). (b) Outer scale region showing hematite (H) and magnetite (M); the H/M interface (dotted white line) displays an irregular morphology. (c) Intermediate oxide layer showing wustite-magnetite mixed region (W+M) containing dispersed Cu-rich occlusions (indicated by white arrows); inset (c)-1 presents higher-magnification view of Cu-rich occlusion particles distributed within the W and M matrix. (d) Steel/scale interface region exhibiting Cu-rich liquid phase formation and Ni-rich region; inset (d)-1 shows detailed microstructure of the subsurface zone containing MnO precipitates, Cr 2 O 3  particles, fayalite (F), and the Cu-rich liquid phase adjacent to the Ni-enriched area; corresponding Cu EDS elemental map confirms the spatial distribution and enrichment of copper within the liquid phase at the interface

Figure  5  shows the cross-sectional microstructure of the oxidized sample PH-A. The oxide scale exhibits a typical multilayered structure consisting of hematite, magnetite, and wustite from the upper surface toward the steel substrate. Magnetite particles dispersed within the wustite matrix are attributed to the partial decomposition of wustite during cooling. [ 21 ]  The thin hematite layer observed at the upper surface is consistent with the relatively low diffusivity of iron ions in magnetite and hematite compared with wustite. [ 22 ]

No continuous Cu-rich phase was observed at the steel/scale interface in sample PH-A. Instead, fine Cu-rich particles were detected within the oxide scale, particularly in regions where wustite and magnetite coexist. EDS analysis [Figure  5 (d)] indicates that particles enriched in both Cu and Ni, suggesting that they are Cu-Ni alloy occlusions .  This behavior is attributed to the relatively low Cu content and elevated Ni concentration, which promote the formation of dispersed Cu–Ni alloy particles rather than a continuous liquid phase. The presence of Ni is therefore considered to suppress interfacial liquid formation by stabilizing Cu in solid solution or as discrete alloy particles. [ 23 , 24 ]

Internal oxidation was also observed beneath the steel/scale interface, where oxides such as fayalite, chromium oxide, and manganese oxide were identified. These oxides form due to the inward diffusion of oxygen and the selective oxidation of alloying elements with higher oxygen affinity than Fe. The distribution of these oxides is governed by the relative diffusion rates of alloying elements, with Mn exhibiting slower diffusion and thus forming fine oxide particles within the steel matrix. [ 25 , 26 ]

In contrast, sample DJ-F exhibited a distinctly different interfacial behavior (Figure  6 ). In addition to the multilayered oxide scale and internal oxidation zone, a Cu-rich liquid phase was clearly observed at the steel/scale interface and along prior-austenite grain boundaries. Although the microstructure observed in Figures  5  and  6  were observed at room-temperature and consist of transformation products such as ferrite and pearlite, the liquid phase penetration occurred at an elevated temperature of 1100 °C. Therefore, the observed penetration paths correspond to prior-austenite grain boundaries. The composition of this phase was identified as a Cu–Sn–Ni alloy, indicating that Sn plays a critical role in lowering the melting temperature and promoting liquid phase formation. The penetration of this liquid phase along grain boundaries provides direct evidence of the mechanism responsible for surface hot shortness.

Thermodynamic calculations were performed to evaluate phase stability as a function of oxygen potential at 1100 °C as shown in Figures  7  and  8 . As the oxygen activity increases, the system transitions from the  γ -Fe stability region to the wustite region, reflecting the selective oxidation of Fe. During this process, Cu is rejected from the growing oxide phase and progressively enriched at the steel/scale interface, leading to the formation of a Cu-rich liquid phase once its solubility limit is exceeded. The calculations predict a significantly higher liquid phase fraction at the interface in sample DJ-F [0.233 wt pct, Figure  8 (a)] compared to sample PH-A [0.122 wt pct, Figure  7 (a)], consistent with the experimental observations. The calculated compositions of the Cu-rich liquid phase also show good agreement with the experimental measurements, supporting the validity of the thermodynamic description. Fig. 7 Thermodynamic calculations of the sample PH-A. ( a ) Phase fractions of oxides and the liquid phase formed as a function of the activity of O 2 . ( b ) Calculated elemental composition of the liquid phase at each activity of O 2 Fig. 8 Thermodynamic calculations of the sample DJ-F. ( a ) Phase fractions of oxides and the liquid phase formed as a function of the activity of O 2 . ( b ) Calculated elemental composition of the liquid phase at each activity of O 2

A systematic comparison across all samples (Table  III ) indicates that Cu-rich interfacial phases formed in most cases, although their morphology and penetration behavior varied with composition. In samples with relatively low effective Cu content, the liquid phase remained as isolated particles at the interface, whereas in samples with higher effective Cu content, penetration along prior-austenite grain boundaries was consistently observed. The penetration of a low-melting Cu-rich liquid phase into grain boundaries severely weakens interfacial cohesion and promotes surface cracking under thermomechanical stress. To link these microstructural observations to macroscopic behavior, Table  III  summarizes the hot shortness susceptibility of each sample based on the observed Cu-rich liquid phase morphology. High susceptibility is assigned to samples exhibiting continuous intergranular liquid penetration, while low susceptibility is assigned to those with isolated liquid particles or suppressed liquid formation. sections.heading: Development of a Copper-Equivalent Parameter
paragraphs: To quantify the formation tendency of the Cu-rich liquid phase, thermodynamic calculations were carried out using a representative base composition (Table  IV ). The effects of Cu, Sn, Ni, As, and S on the liquid phase fraction at the steel/scale interface were systematically evaluated within industrially relevant composition ranges. Table IV Typical Composition of Scrap-Based EAF Steel as a Baseline for Calculations Sample (Wt Pct) Cu Sn Ni As Cr Si Mn P C S N Fe Baseline 0.3 0.015 0.15 0.005 0.2 0.15 0.7 0.02 0.3 0.03 0.01 bal.

A strong linear correlation was observed between Cu eq  and the calculated liquid phase fraction ( R 2  = 0.8959), indicating that the proposed parameter effectively captures the combined effects of tramp elements on interfacial liquid formation.

Unlike previously reported Cu eq  expressions, which are primarily empirical and based on macroscopic observations of surface cracking, the present formulation is derived directly from thermodynamically calculated phase fractions. As a result, the coefficients reflect the intrinsic contribution of each element to the stability of the Cu-rich liquid phase. This physically based formulation provides a more fundamental description of the relationship between composition and interfacial liquid formation.

The negative coefficient of Ni reflects its role in stabilizing Cu in solid solution and suppressing liquid phase formation, whereas Sn exhibits a strong positive coefficient due to its effect on lowering the melting temperature of the Cu-rich phase.

Regarding the multifaceted role of sulfur, the interplay between sulfide formation, the thermodynamic activity of Cu, and the oxidation kinetics is critical for mitigating surface hot shortness. The significant negative coefficient of S (−2.84) in the proposed Cu eq  formula is primarily attributed to the reduction of the effective liquid phase fraction. Specifically, S promotes the precipitation of stable Cu-containing sulfides ( e.g. , Cu 2 S or complex Fe–Cu–S inclusions) at the steel/scale interface. [ 27 , 28 ]  Yamamoto  et al . demonstrated that stable sulfides ( e.g. , MnS) provide effective nucleation sites that trap tramp elements within the matrix. [ 27 ]  Recent studies further confirm that such sulfide precipitation fundamentally alters interfacial behavior and enhances the hot ductility of steels. [ 29 ]  Consequently, these sulfides substantially reduce the thermodynamic activity of Cu at the interface.

Thermodynamically limiting the effective concentration of the liquid phase available for grain boundary penetration is a fundamental principle in controlling embrittlement. This concept is analogous to the mitigation of liquid metal embrittlement (LME), where embrittlement is suppressed by reducing liquid availability via mechanisms like isothermal solidification. [ 17 ]  Similarly, in the present system, stable sulfides act as metallurgical sinks for Cu. This limits the volume fraction of the interfacial liquid, thereby preventing the formation of a continuous, low-melting film that induces severe intergranular cracking.

While the present thermodynamic calculation provide a foundational predictive framework based on local equilibrium, the interfacial behavior during high-temperature oxidation is fundamentally a diffusion-controlled process. The time-dependent enrichment of tramp elements is governed by the dynamic competition between the oxidation rate of Fe and the restricted back-diffusion of elements like Cu and Sn into the steel matrix. [ 30 ]  Once the Cu-rich liquid phase forms, its intergranular penetration occurs when the grain boundary energy (σ GB ) is larger than the solid-liquid interfacial energy (2σ SL ). [ 31 ]  The Cu-rich liquid phase penetration rate is governed by capillary force. [ 32 ]  Moreover, when additional stress is applied to the steel plate, the grain boundary wetting can be accelerated, resulting in wetting transition. [ 33 ]  Therefore, while equilibrium models predict the theoretical liquid fraction, the actual severity of surface hot shortness is dynamically governed by the interplay of diffusion-controlled kinetics, time-dependent enrichment, and stress-assisted wetting transitions, which should be explicitly considered in future model refinements.

sections.heading: Critical Compositional Limit for Surface Hot Shortness
paragraphs: The proposed copper-equivalent parameter was validated by comparing Cu eq  values with experimentally observed liquid phase fractions and penetration behavior (Figure  11 ). Most samples followed the predicted linear trend, confirming the reliability of the proposed relationship. The critical Cu eq  value of 0.245 wt pct was determined by correlating the calculated Cu eq  values with the experimentally observed onset of grain boundary penetration. As shown in Figure  11 , this value corresponds to the intersection point at which the liquid phase fraction becomes sufficient to transition from isolated interfacial particles to continuous liquid film capable of penetrating grain boundaries—a threshold behavior that marks the onset of surface hot shortness. Below this value, the Cu-rich liquid phase remained as discrete particles at the steel/scale interface with no observable intergranular penetration. Above this value, continuous liquid film formation and clear grain boundary penetration were consistently observed. This threshold provides a physically meaningful criterion for assessing hot shortness susceptibility, as it is directly linked to the formation and stability of the interfacial liquid phase. The proposed critical threshold, however, was derived under the specific experimental condition of 1100 °C and an oxidation atmosphere of 85 pct N 2 -10 pct CO 2 -5 pct O 2 . This threshold may vary with changes in reheating temperature and atmosphere. The results suggest that controlling the combined concentration of tramp elements, rather than individual elements, is essential for ensuring hot workability in scrap-based EAF steels. Fig. 11 Correlation between thermodynamically calculated liquid phase fractions and Cu-equivalent values, suggesting the critical upper limit of the proposed Cu-equivalent formula

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This study systematically investigated the effects of tramp element accumulation on surface hot shortness in scrap-based EAF steels, with particular emphasis on the formation and stability of Cu-enriched liquid phases at the steel/oxide interface. High-temperature oxidation experiments revealed that the formation of a Cu-rich liquid phase at the interface is strongly dependent on the combined concentration of tramp elements. In steels with relatively low effective Cu content, Cu was stabilized as dispersed particles within the oxide scale, whereas in steels with higher effective Cu content, a continuous Cu-rich liquid phase formed and penetrated along prior-austenite grain boundaries. This penetration behavior provides direct evidence of the mechanism responsible for surface hot shortness during hot working. Thermodynamic calculations successfully reproduced both the phase constitution and the composition of the Cu-rich liquid phase under conditions relevant to high-temperature oxidation. The good agreement between experimental observations and thermodynamic predictions confirms that the formation of interfacial liquid phases can be quantitatively assessed based on phase stability considerations. Based on this framework, a copper-equivalent parameter was developed to represent the combined effects of major tramp elements, including Cu, Sn, Ni, As, and S. The proposed parameter shows a strong linear correlation with the fraction of the Cu-rich liquid phase, demonstrating its effectiveness in quantifying hot shortness susceptibility. A critical threshold of approximately 0.245 wt pct in the copper-equivalent value was identified, above which grain boundary penetration of the liquid phase becomes significant. The results of this study establish a physically grounded criterion for evaluating surface hot shortness in scrap-based steels. The proposed approach provides a practical tool for controlling tramp element levels and optimizing scrap utilization in EAF steelmaking, while maintaining adequate hot workability.
